title: Le Nozze di Figaro
facts: Le nozze di Figaro premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna on 1 May 1786.
Beaumarchais’s play was at first banned in Vienna for its frank treatment of class conflict; Da Ponte won the emperor’s approval for an opera version.
It was Mozart who picked Beaumarchais’s play. Da Ponte turned it into a libretto in six weeks, removing all of the political references.
Aprite un po|Tutto è disposto|Tutto e disposto
Da Ponte swapped Figaro’s angry speech against inherited nobility for an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives.
Mozart uses two horns playing together here to represent cuckoldry. Verdi later borrowed the same trick in Falstaff.
The first-night audience demanded encores of five numbers; on 8 May, seven.
Worried about the running time, Emperor Joseph II ordered posters announcing that no piece for more than a single voice was to be repeated.
A 1786 Vienna review: Mozart’s music was admired by connoisseurs, but “obstreperous louts in the uppermost storey” tried to drown out the singers.
In Prague the opera caused a sensation; a local paper wrote that “no piece … has ever caused such a sensation.” That success led to the commission of Don Giovanni.
The Act II finale runs about 20 minutes, one of the longest uninterrupted pieces of music Mozart ever wrote.
Brahms: “In my opinion, each number in Figaro is a miracle … nothing like it was ever done again, not even by Beethoven.”
Mozart liked this tune enough to quote “Non più andrai” in the second act of Don Giovanni.
“Porgi, amor” reuses the motif that opens Mozart’s early bassoon concerto.
Cosa sento|Così fan tutte|Cosi fan tutte
Basilio’s phrase “Così fan tutte le belle” in this trio later turned up in the overture to Mozart’s Così fan tutte.
Beethoven wrote a set of variations for violin and piano on Figaro’s “Se vuol ballare”.
For a 1789 revival Mozart wrote two replacement arias for Susanna. The Met used them in 1998, with Cecilia Bartoli as Susanna.
